title: Family and the word for "of"
goal: Talk about your family — and master the two ways of showing possession that make Egyptian much friendlier than Fusha: attached endings and the stand-alone word بتاع.
bekal: name family members and ask about other people's families
attach the possessive endings ـي، ـك، ـه، ـها to nouns

dialogs.title: حوار — صور على الموبايل
dialogs.intro: In the institute cafeteria. Mona shows Budi a photo of her family on her phone, and Budi replies with one of his own.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: Look, this is a photo of my family.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ما شاء الله! عيلة كبيرة. دول مين؟
lines.id: Mashallah! A big family. Who are they?

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: ده بابا، ودي ماما. ودول إخواتي.
lines.baca: da baaba, wi di maama. wi dōl ikhwaati.
lines.id: This is my dad, and this is my mom. And these are my brothers and sisters.
lines.literal: this dad, and this mom. and these my-siblings.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: How many brothers and sisters do you have?
lines.literal: at-you how-many brother and how-many sister?

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: عندي أخ واحد وأختين. أنا الكبيرة.
lines.baca: ‘andi akh waahid wi ukhtēn. ana l-kibiira.
lines.id: I have one brother and two sisters. I'm the oldest.
lines.literal: at-me brother one and two-sisters. I the-big(f).

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: And what does your dad do?

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: بابا دكتور، وماما مدرسة في مدرسة ابتدائي.
lines.baca: baaba duktuur, wi maama mudarrisa fi madrasa ibtidaa’i.
lines.id: Dad's a doctor, and Mom teaches at a primary school.
lines.literal: dad doctor, and mom teacher(f) in school primary.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: حلو. أنا عندي أخت واحدة بس.
lines.id: Nice. I only have one sister.
lines.literal: sweet. I at-me sister one only.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.baca: wi hiyya akbar minnak walla aṣghar?
lines.id: Is she older or younger than you?
lines.literal: and she bigger than-you or smaller?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أصغر مني بأربع سنين. اسمها ديوي.
lines.baca: aṣghar minni bi-arba‘ siniin. ismaha Dewi.
lines.id: Four years younger than me. Her name's Dewi.
lines.literal: smaller than-me by-four years. her-name Dewi.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Not yet. She's still at university.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: And you? Married or not yet?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: لسه. الأول الشغل، بعدين إن شاء الله.
lines.id: Not yet. Work first, later God willing.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: May God make it easy. You must miss your family.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: A lot. But I call them every day.

notes: **The words بابا and ماما are used even by adults.** In Egypt, a forty-year-old man still says بابا when talking about his father — much like "Dad" in English. The formal forms are أبويا *abuuya* and أمي *ummi*, but both sound a little distant.

**The word عند means "have", and literally "at".** Egyptian has no verb "to have" at all; there's just a preposition with an ending attached. عندي كتاب is literally "at-me a book", and that's how you say "I have a book".

**The word لسه covers two different meanings: "still" and "not yet".** لسه في الجامعة means "still at university", while لسه on its own as an answer means "not yet". Context tells them apart, and Egyptians use it dozens of times a day.
**The word ولا means "or" in questions.** متجوز ولا لسه؟ (married or not yet?). For "or" in statements people use أو *aw* — but ولا is heard far more often.

**Look at بيوحش, which appears here as حتوحشك.** This verb works backwards compared with English "miss": the subject is the one **being missed**, not the one missing. عيلتك حتوحشك is literally "your family will make-you-miss (them)", meaning you're the one who'll miss them.

**The phrase ربنا يسهل is an everyday wish, not a special religious formula.** It means "may God make it easy", and it's used for anything someone is waiting for: a wedding, a job, graduation, recovery. The reply is آمين *aamiin*.

grammars.title: Possessive endings — attached to the noun
body: The first way to show possession is to attach an ending directly to the noun. The same endings are later used on prepositions and as verb objects, so you'll come back to this table again and again.
after: Feminine nouns ending in ـة change slightly: ـة becomes ـت before an ending. So عربية becomes عربيتي *‘arabeyyeti*, and مدرسة becomes مدرستنا *madrastina*.

To negate عند, don't use مش but the wrapper مـ...ـش, as in ماعنديش *ma‘andiish* (I don't have) and ماعندهاش *ma‘andahaash* (she doesn't have). It's treated like a verb, which makes sense — here عند stands in for the verb "have".
The word عند also means "at someone's place": عند الدكتور (at the doctor's), عندنا (at our place). The two meanings live side by side without ever confusing Egyptians.

grammars.title: The word بتاع — a stand-alone "of"
body: The second way is the word بتاع, which works much like English "of mine / of yours" or "'s". It's one of Egyptian's biggest gifts to learners.
after: Notice that بتاع agrees with **the thing owned**, not the owner. الشنطة بتاعتي uses بتاعة because the bag is feminine, even if the owner is a man.

When do you use an ending and when بتاع? For body parts, family, and names — almost always an ending: إيدي، أختي، اسمي. For possessions that can change hands — usually بتاع, as in العربية بتاعتي، الموبايل بتاعك. Both are correct, and Egyptians often use both for the same word.

blocks.text: Notice that Egyptian distinguishes uncles on the father's side from those on the mother's — عم versus خال — like Arabic in general, and unlike English, which calls both "uncle". On the other hand, Egyptian doesn't separate older and younger siblings any more than English does: أخ is a brother, older or younger. To be specific, people add أخويا الكبير (my older brother) or أخويا الصغير.

blocks.title: Forms that change when an ending is added
items: The words أب، أخ، وجوز change slightly when they take an ending: أبويا *abuuya* (my father), أخويا *akhuuya* (my brother), جوزها *goẓa* (her husband). This only happens with a handful of words, so just learn them.
The word مرات is a special form of مرة that only appears in possession: مراتي (my wife), مرات أحمد (Ahmad's wife). It never stands alone.
The word عيال means "kids" in the sense of offspring, and it sounds warm and casual. The more neutral form is أولاد *awlaad*.

sections.title: Asking about family without giving offense

blocks.text: In Egypt, asking about someone's family isn't prying — it's a way of showing you care. The following phrases are safe to use with anyone you've just met.

head: مصري
Say it
Meaning
rows: do you have a big family?
how many brothers do you have?
are you the oldest or the youngest?
say hello to the family for me
may God keep them for you

blocks.text: The last two aren't empty politeness. The phrase سلملي على العيلة is used every time you part from someone whose family you know, and leaving it out feels cold. And ربنا يخليهملك is a warm reply whenever someone mentions their parents or children — the closest English is something like "bless them".

items: This is a photo of my family.
How many brothers do you have? (to a woman)
My dad is a doctor and my mom is a teacher.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right possessive ending.
Rewrite these using بتاع in the right form.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: دي صورة العيلة بتاعتي. — عندك كام أخ؟ — عندي أخت واحدة بس. — بابا دكتور وماما مدرسة. — الكتاب ده بتاع مين؟
الكتاب ده بتاعي. — الشنطة دي بتاعة منى. — العربية دي بتاعة بابا. — الكتب دي بتوعنا. — الموبايل ده بتاع مين؟
دي صورة العيلة بتاعتي. — عندك كام أخ؟ — عندي أخت واحدة بس. — هي أكبر منك ولا أصغر؟ — هي لسه في الجامعة.
